chunks: Prioritizing test points when space is short. The question: If you're short on board space, how do you prioritize which signals should have test points?
Space on a board is limited, so you cannot give every net a test point.
You rank the nets by how much each point is worth compared with what it costs, and you give pads to the highest-ranked ones first.
For the nets you skip, you write down how they are covered another way and what risk remains.
Think of packing a small suitcase for a trip. You pack the passport, phone and medicine first, because the trip fails without them. Then comfort items, and last the nice-to-haves.
If space runs out, you leave the extras at home, and you plan what you will do without them.
Choosing test points works the same way: essentials first, extras only if there is room.
The prioritisation flow. Mandatory items are removed from the competition first, then alternatives are subtracted, and only the leftover candidates are scored.
Net: all the copper that forms one electrical connection. Power rail: a net that carries a supply voltage.
Fixture pin: each test point on a factory fixture needs its own spring pin, which adds cost.
Boundary scan and built-in self-test: ways for chips to test connections without a pad. Fallback: another way the fault would still be caught if a net gets no pad.
Score each net from 1 to 5 for likelihood of a fault (L), severity (S) and unique information (I), then divide by cost (C). Score = L x S x I / C. The 3.
3 volts supply rail scores 5 x 5 x 5 / 1 = 125, so it gets a pad. A crystal, the part that sets a chip's clock, scores 2 x 1 x 1 / 5 = 0.
4, so it gets none, because a probe can stop it from running. Programming lines get pads anyway, since the factory needs them. That is the whole idea.
"I'd rank nets by value over cost. Value is fault likelihood times severity times how much information the pad gives that nothing else does.
Cost is area, signal-integrity impact and a fixture pin. That puts ground, main rails, reset, power-good and programming at the top, then clocks, console and key analog nodes.
I'd make space by sharing connector pins, using boundary scan or firmware readback, and bottom-side pad fields, and I'd review the list with the factory."
